messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Officer Katarina Volkov

Katarina Volkov was thirty-two months into her career with the metropolitan police department when the training scenario went catastrophically wrong. It was meant to be a routine firearms exercise in the basement range—a controlled environment, full safety protocols, her supervising sergeant standing ten feet away. The trainee officer beside her had been certified, or so everyone believed. When his weapon discharged into her abdomen at point-blank range, the impact threw her backward against the cinder-block wall. She remembered the sergeant's face frozen in shock, the acrid smell of cordite, the sensation of her own blood spreading warm across her ribs before the pain arrived. What she remembered most, though—what returned to her unbidden in the weeks that followed—was the moment she realized the weapon had been loaded with live rounds. The trainee had not checked. No one had checked. The people she had trusted to keep her safe had failed her in the most fundamental way.

The physical injuries healed within four months. The bullet had missed her spleen by centimeters; she was told she was lucky. But by the time Katarina returned to light duty in the autumn, something had fractured that no surgeon could repair. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt unshakeable, that her own body was a traitor. Her heart would race without warning—in the grocery store, at a red light, sitting on the couch beside her girlfriend Marcus. Her hands would tremble when she held a coffee cup. Her breathing would shallow and quicken as though her lungs had forgotten how to work. These reactions made no sense to her. She was safe. She was home. Yet her body insisted, moment after moment, that danger was imminent and closing in. What terrified her most was that she could not trust herself anymore. If her body could betray her like this, how could she rely on it to protect her? How could she trust anyone else when the institution she had devoted herself to had failed so catastrophically?

The memories came without warning, vivid and complete. When they arrived, Katarina was no longer in her apartment in November 2024; she was back in that basement range, the fluorescent lights humming overhead, the smell of gun oil and concrete filling her nostrils, the weight of the sergeant's stare. The sensations were so immediate and overwhelming that she would sometimes find herself on the floor, unsure how she had gotten there. What made it worse was that these memories felt profoundly alien to her—as though they belonged to someone else, some other woman who had been shot, not to Katarina herself. She would watch herself in these moments from a distance, seeing her own hands shaking, her own chest heaving, as though observing a stranger in crisis. The detachment was almost as disorienting as the vividness. She could not control when the memories forced their way in. They came while she was driving, while she was trying to sleep, while Marcus was speaking to her and her mind simply vanished into that basement without permission.

Over the following months, Katarina's sense of the world had shifted into something darker and more fragile. The precinct, once a place of purpose and belonging, now felt like a minefield of incompetence and negligence. She was certain that danger lurked in ordinary moments—that the next mistake, the next oversight, the next betrayal by someone she had to trust, was always seconds away. When she returned to full duty in January, she found herself hypervigilant in ways that exhausted her. Every sound in the station made her flinch. Every interaction with her colleagues carried an undercurrent of suspicion. She trusted no one to check equipment, to follow protocol, to keep her safe. This wariness, this conviction that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that people would inevitably fail her, seemed to reach backward and intensify the memories themselves. The more certain she became that danger was omnipresent, the more forcefully the basement memory intruded, as if her mind was trying to prove to her that her fears were justified. The memories and her appraisals had become locked in a vicious cycle: each one feeding the other, each one making the other feel more real, more true, more inescapable.

By October, Katarina had begun avoiding shifts that required her to work in the basement, making excuses to her sergeant that she knew were transparent. She had stopped going to the gun range entirely—a decision that had begun to isolate her from her unit and raise questions about her fitness for duty. Marcus had noticed the withdrawal too, the way Katarina would tense when sirens passed their apartment, the way she had stopped sleeping more than a few hours at a time. When Marcus tried to hold her at night, Katarina would feel her body stiffen, her breathing quicken, as though she were being threatened rather than comforted. She had not told Marcus the full extent of what was happening—the intrusive memories, the sense of unreality, the conviction that her own body was working against her. She was afraid that if she spoke it aloud, it would become even more true. It was only last week, when she had called in sick for the fourth time in two weeks and her lieutenant had asked her directly if she needed to see someone, that Katarina had finally admitted to herself that she could not manage this alone. She had come to her first therapy appointment carrying the weight of a betrayal so complete that she had begun to wonder whether she could ever trust her own mind again.
